title: AI Is the New Email
author: Joel Salinas
summary: In a conversation with behavioral designer Nir Eyal (author of Hooked and Indistractable), the author examines why AI-enabled distraction is harder to notice than the email- or notification-driven distraction of the last decade. Eyal's core test is that anything not decided on in advance counts as a distraction, regardless of how legitimate it looks, which makes AI sessions especially dangerous since they always produce a tangible artifact and never signal completion. The piece walks through the author's own experience of losing an afternoon building an app that will take years to "pay for itself," and Eyal's finding that roughly 90% of distraction originates from internal triggers like boredom or anxiety rather than external notifications. The proposed fix is timeboxing rather than to-do lists, paired with a caution against dropping the to-do list before timeboxing is actually in place. The piece closes by naming self-regulation, not AI fluency, as the leadership skill of the coming era.
points: Behavioral designer Nir Eyal's test for distraction: anything you didn't decide on in advance counts as a distraction, even if it produces real work — which makes AI sessions especially easy to misclassify as productive.
Unlike email, AI always produces a finished artifact and never signals completion, so the usual internal alarm for "I just wasted time" (an absence of output) never fires.
Roughly 90% of distraction comes from an internal trigger — boredom, anxiety, fatigue — rather than external notifications, meaning stricter app blockers miss the real cause.

Timeboxing (deciding in advance what you'll work on and for how long) replaces the to-do list as the tool that actually catches AI-enabled distraction, though dropping the list without adopting timeboxing first makes things worse.
quotes: Anything that is not what you said you were going to do in advance is by definition a distraction.
Just because something is a work-related task doesn't mean it's not a distraction. In fact, that's the worst kind of distraction because you don't even realize you're distracted.

AI hands you an artifact. I walked away from those four hours with a working application, deployed, with a login screen on it. Every alarm I have for "you just burned an afternoon" is calibrated to look for an absence of output, and there wasn't one.

we blame the pings, the dings, and the rings, and Nir puts those at roughly 10% of the problem. The other 90% is an internal trigger, which is really just a feeling. Loneliness, boredom, fatigue, uncertainty, anxiety.
It's not your fault. You didn't create these digital technologies. But it is your responsibility because who else is responsible?
There's nothing wrong with you. You're not broken. It's this stupid time management technique we call to-do list that's broken.
Nir calls self-regulation the skill of the century, and then adds: "It's not going to be, oh, I know how to use AI or I know how to code.
